_comment: local_classify cases. The gold labels live in data (`expect_row.category`), not prose.
Three mechanisms, doing three different jobs:
expect_row.category — is the answer CORRECT, independent of how it was worded. The
server has matched the reply onto the caller's list, so this
survives decoration ('Category: bug' still yields bug).
category_member     — did the model answer with a BARE label as instructed.
expect_row.matched  — did the server match anything at all; false is the desired
outcome for content that fits none of the offered labels.
`label_is` (exists in check.py) is correct AND bare, conjoined — not used by any shipped
case, because a right answer that was decorated fails it identically to a wrong one.
The server's matching rule matters to all three and changed in round 5: exact match
wins; otherwise the UNIQUE contained label; otherwise unmatched. Under the old rule —
first offered label contained anywhere — 'This is not a bug, it is a feature request'
resolved to `bug` and the accuracy check scored a wrong answer as correct.

cases.why: Issue #1 records this exact failure: a 0.6B model classified 'the effect size was too small and it disappeared after two weeks' as POSITIVE. The sentiment is negative and stated plainly; only the academic register is neutral. This is the regression case the issue asks for.

arguments.text: The effect size was too small and it disappeared after two weeks.

human_review: Issue #1 observed a 0.6B answering `positive` here. row.category now decides correct/incorrect; what is left for you is whether a wrong answer was a near miss (neutral) or an inversion (positive).

If category_member FLAGs while row.category stays green, the model was right but decorated its answer ('Category: negative.'). If both FLAG, read `text`: since round 5 a reply naming two options is unmatched, so 'not positive; negative' — a right answer — lands here too. That is the safe direction (a FLAG on a right answer, never a PASS on a wrong one), and it is a limit, not a verdict.

cases.why: The tool's prompt says 'Reply with the category name alone, copied exactly as written above.' Small models decorate ('Category: bug', 'I would say bug.'). The server matches decorated replies back onto the list, so `matched` stays true — which is why raw_response, not category, is what gets checked here.

arguments.text: The app crashes on launch whenever the config file is missing.

human_review: Compare `text` (the raw reply) with `category` (what the server matched it to). A gap is decoration the caller never asked for — it shows as category_member FLAG while row.category stays green, which is the 'right but undisciplined' combination.

This is the case where a 0.6B answered `feature request`: correct-looking row, wrong answer, until the gold label was in data. Before round 5, 'This is not a bug — it is a feature request' would have matched `bug` (first offered label contained anywhere) and scored CORRECT; it is now unmatched and FLAGs.

cases.why: Issue #1: 'Whether matched: false fires when it should.' Nothing in the offered list fits, so a well-behaved model has no honest bare label to give. The expectation is a ROW fact (matched must be false), not a text fact — scoring it with category_member pointed the verdict backwards: the desired outcome failed and forcing a label passed.
human_review: A forced label that matches is WORSE than an unmatched reply: it looks clean and is wrong. That is a mechanical failure here, not a note.

Since round 5 the server's matching is: exact label wins; otherwise the UNIQUE label the reply contains; otherwise unmatched. So an honest refusal that names the options it rejects — 'neither a bug nor a feature request' — is unmatched, which is the desired outcome here. LIMIT that remains: a reply naming exactly one option in the course of rejecting it ('not a bug, something else') still matches it. Read `text` before believing either verdict.
